newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to leave area bigger than Belgium fallow.
newsitem.headline: EU to leave area bigger than Belgium fallow.

text.p: The European Commission proposed on Thursday taking an area bigger than Belgium and Luxembourg put together out of cereals production next year.
Cereals farmers who want to claim EU subsidies will have to leave five percent of their arable farmland fallow between July 1998 and June 1999, a figure unchanged from this season.
Altogther that would leave an estimated two million hectares of land idle. Another 2.5 million hectares are expected to be taken out of production under a separate volontary set-aside scheme.
"It's in line with requests from EU farm ministers last month but is not in response to those requests," Commission agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely said.
Farm ministers last month unanimously demanded an unchanged five percent set-aside rate but EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler refused to be rushed, saying he needed more crop data.
France, the EU's main grain exporter, said a low set-aside rate would allow farmers to exploit their production potential and strengthen Europe's position on the world market.
Germany, which originally wanted 10 percent, said it could live with the proposal.

"It's good news," said an official from COPA, the EU farmers organisation, stressing that the European Parliament and EU farm ministers should give their approval this month so that farmers could plan autumn plantings.
The Commission said that an unchanged set-aside rate would help to keep supply and demand in balance and safeguard against drought and other climatic problems.
"It's necessary to maintain production potential without...rebuilding excessive public stocks," it said in a statement.
Spokesman Kiely added that preliminary estimates from various organisations pointed to a slightly lower cereals crop of between 197 to 200 million tonnes in 1997.
On Friday Coceral, the EU grain trade lobby, forecast an EU grain crop of 197.29 million tonnes in 1997/98, against last season's record 201.54 million.
Consumption could perhaps increase further in 1997/98 following a substantial rise last season, Kiely said, adding that cereals prices were expected to be lower.
Export prospects were also seen to be bullish after subsidised shipments nearly tripled to 27 million tonnes in 1996/97.
"The outlook for cereals exports is fairly positive," Kiely said.
In line with EU farm ministers' demands, the Commission proposed suspending so-called penalty set-aside, for exceeding area limits, for another year to June 30, 1998.
It also proposed to ease penalties for exceeding cereals planting limits on irrigated land.

Compulsory set-aside is a controversial farm reform agreed in 1992 to help remove costly grain surpluses. It was originally set at 15 percent but gradually lowered after drought hit crops and stocks plunged.
Farmers and grain traders attack set-aside because it curbs their earnings. Taxpayers and environmentalists criticise huge payments to farmers for doing nothing and risk land returning to wilderness.
